source.text: Kumārajīva, trans., Lotus Sutra, chapter 16, The Lifespan of the Tathāgata (Taishō T262): selections from the prose, and the closing verses in full

yr01.heading: Told Three Times to Believe, Asked Three Times
yr01.plain: Then the Buddha said to the bodhisattvas and the whole assembly: "Good sons, you should believe and understand the true words of the Tathāgata." Again he said to the assembly: "You should believe and understand the true words of the Tathāgata." And once more he said: "You should believe and understand the true words of the Tathāgata." Then the bodhisattvas, led by Maitreya, joined their palms and said: "World-Honored One, please tell us. We will believe and accept the Buddha's words." They asked three times like this and then said again: "Please tell us. We will believe and accept the Buddha's words."
yr01.commentary: The Buddha says the same thing three times, and the assembly asks four times. That shows how hard to believe and how important what follows is. It is the gateway to the deepest secret of the Lotus Sutra.

yr02.heading: Awakening Did Not First Happen at Gayā
yr02.plain: Then the World-Honored One, knowing that the bodhisattvas had asked three times and would not stop, said: "Listen well to the Tathāgata's secret and spiritual power. All the gods, humans and asuras of the world think that the present Śākyamuni Buddha left the palace of the Śākyas, sat at the place of awakening not far from the city of Gayā, and attained supreme awakening. But good sons, in truth it has been boundless, endless hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of kalpas since I became a Buddha."
yr02.commentary: The central declaration of this chapter. People know the Buddha as first awakening beneath the bodhi tree at thirty-five, but in fact he became a Buddha immeasurably long ago. This is called "Buddhahood attained in the distant past."

yr03.heading: The Parable of the Dust Motes
yr03.plain: "Suppose someone ground five hundred thousand million nayuta asaṃkhyeya great trichiliocosms into dust, and went east, dropping one mote each time they passed five hundred thousand million nayuta asaṃkhyeya lands, until the dust was used up. … If all the worlds passed through, whether a mote was dropped there or not, were ground into dust and each mote counted as one kalpa, the time since I became a Buddha would exceed even that by hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya kalpas."
yr03.commentary: Piling unimaginably large numbers on top of each other, it shows that the Buddha's life has no end. This parable is called "the kalpas of five hundred dust motes." The weight is less on the size of the numbers than on the meaning that the Buddha has always been with us.

yr04.heading: Always Teaching in This World
yr04.plain: "Since then I have always dwelt in this Sahā world, teaching the Dharma and transforming beings, and in hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya other lands I have also guided and benefited beings."
yr04.commentary: The Buddha is not someone far away; he is always teaching in this very world of suffering (the Sahā world). This line grounds the Lotus Sutra faith that "the Buddha is here, now."

yr05.heading: The World as the Tathāgata Sees It
yr05.plain: "The Tathāgata knows and sees the marks of the three realms just as they are. In them there is no birth or death, no retreating or appearing, no one who stays in the world and no one who enters nirvana. They are neither true nor false, neither the same nor different; he does not see the three realms as the beings of the three realms see them. The Tathāgata sees such things clearly and without error. … Thus it has been very long since I became a Buddha; my life is measureless asaṃkhyeya kalpas, always abiding and never perishing."
yr05.commentary: Beings see the world divided into birth and death, existence and non-existence, but the Tathāgata sees the reality beyond. That is why the Buddha's life too is not something that will end one day, but ever-abiding and imperishable.

yr06.heading: Why He Shows Nirvana
yr06.plain: "If the Buddha stayed long in the world, people of thin virtue would not plant good roots; they would live poor and lowly, sink into the five desires, and enter the net of false thoughts and wrong views. Seeing that the Tathāgata always remains and never passes away, they would grow proud and self-indulgent, weary and lazy, and would not feel that he is hard to meet or have a reverent heart. So the Tathāgata says as a skillful means: Monks, know that it is hard to meet a Buddha appearing in the world."
yr06.commentary: This answers why, if the Buddha is always present, he entered nirvana. If people think they can meet him any time, they grow lazy. Only with the feeling that he is hard to meet again do they seek the teaching earnestly. Nirvana is a skillful means to awaken beings.

yr07.heading: The Parable of the Good Doctor (1): Children Who Drank Poison
yr07.plain: "Suppose there was a good doctor, wise and clever, versed in medicines and remedies, who healed every kind of illness. He had ten, twenty, even a hundred children. While he was away in a distant land on business, his children drank someone else's poison; the poison spread, and they lost their senses and rolled on the ground. Then their father came home. Of the children who had drunk poison, some had lost their right minds and some had not, but seeing their father from afar they all rejoiced greatly, bowed, knelt and said: 'Welcome home safely. In our foolishness we drank poison by mistake. Please heal us and give us back our lives.'"
yr07.commentary: This is the parable of the good doctor, one of the seven parables of the Lotus Sutra. The good doctor is the Buddha, the children are beings, and the poison is the affliction of greed, anger and delusion.

yr08.heading: The Parable of the Good Doctor (2): Children Who Won't Take the Medicine
yr08.plain: "Seeing his children suffering like this, the father followed his prescriptions, found good medicinal herbs complete in color, fragrance and flavor, pounded, sifted and mixed them, and gave them to his children. … Those who had not lost their right minds saw the medicine of good color and fragrance, took it at once, and were completely healed. But those who had lost their minds, though glad their father had come and asking him to heal them, would not take the medicine when he gave it. Why? The poison had gone deep and they had lost their right minds, so they thought this medicine of good color and fragrance tasted bad."
yr08.commentary: Even with good medicine (the teaching) before them, when afflictions run deep people do not see that it is good. It sharply reflects how we long for rescue yet refuse it.

yr09.heading: The Parable of the Good Doctor (3): News of the Father's Death
yr09.plain: "The father thought: '… Now I must use a skillful means to make them take this medicine.' And he said: 'Know this: I am old now and my time to die has come. I leave this good medicine here; take it. Do not worry that you will not get well.' Having told them this, he went again to another land and sent a messenger to say, 'Your father has died.' Hearing that their father had died, the children grieved deeply … and, sunk always in sorrow, at last their minds awoke. Only then did they see that this medicine was good in color, flavor and fragrance, and took it, and the illness of the poison was completely healed. Hearing that his children had all recovered, the father returned at once and showed himself to them all."
yr09.commentary: The father's "death" was a skillful means to awaken his children. The Buddha's nirvana is the same: the sorrow of the Buddha's leaving wakes us up to take the teaching (medicine) he left behind. The Buddha then asks whether this doctor can be said to have lied, and the assembly answers no.

yr10.heading: Verses of Eternal Life (1): I Always Teach Here
yr10.plain: Since I became a Buddha, the kalpas that have passed are measureless hundreds of thousands of millions of asaṃkhyeyas. For measureless kalpas I have always taught the Dharma, transforming countless millions of beings and leading them onto the Buddha way. To save beings, as a skillful means I showed nirvana, but in truth I did not pass away; I always dwell here teaching the Dharma. I always dwell here, but with my spiritual powers I make beings of upside-down thinking unable to see me, though I am near.
yr10.commentary: The verses at the end of this chapter, named after their opening words as "Verses of Eternal Life" (Jaga-ge). They are the best-known verses chanted daily by followers of the Lotus Sutra. "Though I am near, they do not see me" reminds us that the Buddha is not far away; we simply do not see.

yr11.heading: Verses of Eternal Life (2): Appearing Together on Vulture Peak
yr11.plain: Seeing that I entered nirvana, beings make offerings widely to my relics, and all feel longing and thirsting reverence. When beings have faith and follow, with straight and gentle minds, single-mindedly wishing to see the Buddha, not sparing even their lives, then I appear with the Sangha on Vulture Peak and say to beings: 'I am always here and do not pass away. By the power of skillful means I show passing away and not passing away.' If in other lands there are beings who revere, believe and rejoice,
yr11.commentary: When beings long earnestly for the Buddha and their minds become straight and gentle, the Buddha shows himself again. The condition for meeting the Buddha is not a place but the mind. Vulture Peak is where the Lotus Sutra was taught.

yr12.heading: Verses of Eternal Life (3): In the Sea of Suffering
yr12.plain: I also teach the supreme Dharma among them. You do not hear it and think only that I have entered nirvana. I see beings sunk in suffering, so I deliberately do not show my body, making them feel thirsting reverence. When their hearts are full of longing, only then do I appear and teach the Dharma. Such is my spiritual power that for asaṃkhyeya kalpas I always dwell on Vulture Peak and in many other places. Even when beings see the kalpa ending and everything burning in the great fire,
yr12.commentary: Even the Buddha hiding his form is compassion, because only when longing deepens is the teaching engraved deeply in the heart.

yr13.heading: Verses of Eternal Life (4): The Indestructible Pure Land
yr13.plain: this land of mine is at peace, always full of gods and humans, its gardens, groves, halls and pavilions adorned with every kind of jewel. Jewel trees are full of flowers and fruit where beings wander and delight; the gods beat heavenly drums and always play all kinds of music, and rain down māndārava flowers scattering them over the Buddha and the assembly. My Pure Land is not destroyed, yet beings see it all burned up, and sorrow, fear and every suffering fill it. These beings full of wrongdoing, through the causes of evil karma, pass asaṃkhyeya kalpas without even hearing the name of the Three Jewels. But those who cultivate merit and are gentle and straight,
yr13.commentary: The same world is a burning place to some and a peaceful Pure Land to others. The world does not change; the seeing mind differs. It holds the Lotus Sutra's view of the Pure Land: "this land is the Pure Land."

yr14.heading: Verses of Eternal Life (5): Like the Doctor's Skillful Means
yr14.plain: all see me here teaching the Dharma. Sometimes to this assembly I teach that the Buddha's life is measureless; to those who meet the Buddha only after a long time, I teach that a Buddha is hard to meet. Such is the power of my wisdom that the light of wisdom shines without limit, and a life of countless kalpas was gained through long cultivation. You who are wise, do not doubt this; cut off doubt and end it forever. The Buddha's words are true, not false. Just as the doctor used a good skillful means to heal his deranged children,
yr14.commentary: Saying "the Buddha is eternal" to some and "the Buddha is hard to meet" to others is not a contradiction but skillful means. Both come from the single wish to heal beings.

yr15.heading: Verses of Eternal Life (6): How Can I Help Beings
yr15.plain: and could not be called a liar though he was alive and said he had died, so I too, as father of the world, save those who suffer. Because ordinary people are lost in upside-down thinking, though I truly remain, I say I have entered nirvana. For if they always saw me, they would grow proud and self-indulgent, become lazy, cling to the five desires and fall into evil paths. I always know whether beings practice the Way or not, and according to what will save them I teach all kinds of Dharma. I always think to myself: 'How can I lead beings to enter supreme wisdom and swiftly attain the body of a Buddha?'
yr15.commentary: The last four lines of these verses, "I always think to myself: how can I lead beings to enter supreme wisdom and swiftly attain the body of a Buddha?", are widely loved for showing the Buddha's heart in a word. Not for a moment does the Buddha stop thinking how everyone might become a Buddha.

maitreya.definition: The bodhisattva who will become the next Buddha after Śākyamuni. The name means "the loving one."

anuttara-bodhi.definition: Supreme, right and complete awakening: the awakening of a Buddha.

nayuta.definition: An ancient Indian unit for a very large number, said to be a hundred billion or a trillion.

asamkhya.definition: A very large number meaning "uncountable": anything immeasurably many or long.

kalpa.definition: An immeasurably long span of time; also one cycle of a world's forming and destruction.

saha.definition: "The world of endurance": this world of ours, where we live bearing suffering, and where Śākyamuni Buddha teaches.

three-realms.definition: The three worlds beings are born and die in: the desire realm, the form realm without desire, and the formless realm.

upaya.definition: Upāya: wise ways of leading beings to the teaching, suited to their capacities and circumstances. One of the central ideas of the Lotus Sutra.

five-desires.definition: Desire for the five sense objects (sights, sounds, smells, tastes, touches), or for wealth, sex, food, fame and sleep.

gridhrakuta.definition: Gṛdhrakūṭa, a mountain near Rājagṛha in India, named for its vulture-shaped peak; where the Lotus Sutra was taught.

sarira.definition: Śarīra: the remains of a Buddha or saint, enshrined in stupas and honored with offerings.

three-jewels.definition: The three treasures of Buddhism: the Buddha, the Dharma (teaching) and the Sangha (community of practitioners).
